body.text: Subsection 127(9) of Canada’s Income Tax Act sets out the key investment tax credit definitions for SR&ED claimants, including “investment tax credit”, “qualified expenditure”, shared-use equipment and, under Bill C-15, “eligible Canadian public corporation”. It sets the 15% basic ITC rate, with a 20-year carryforward and 3-year carryback for unused credits.

Canada’s Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive regime has undergone its most substantial legislative and administrative expansion in over a decade following the enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026.

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024), Bill C-15 codifies four structural reforms to the federal SR&ED program initially proposed in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and expanded in the 2025 Federal Budget (Canada Strong, November 4, 2025). First, the maximum annual qualified expenditure limit eligible for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) has doubled from $3,000,000 (and the interim $4,500,000 proposal in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement) to $6,000,000, increasing the maximum annual cash refund on current expenditures from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000. Second, the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada phase-out range for Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) has widened from the former $10,000,000–$50,000,000 bracket to $15,000,000–$75,000,000 under amended subsection 127(10.2) of the Income Tax Act. Third, access to the enhanced 35% refundable ITC has been extended for the first time to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) as defined in subsection 127(9), subject to a $15,000,000–$75,000,000 phase-out based on three-year average annual gross revenue under subsection 127(10.6), while standalone and associated CCPCs may now elect under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) to compute their expenditure limit using this three-year average gross revenue test rather than taxable capital. Fourth, eligibility for depreciable capital property (paragraph 37(1)(b)), first-term and second-term Shared-Use Equipment (SUE, subsection 127(9)), and equipment lease expenditures has been restored for property acquired and available for use, or lease costs first becoming payable, after December 15, 2024.

Simultaneously, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an elective Pre-Claim Approval (PCA) process providing eligible businesses (with under $25,000,000 in annual gross income) with upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks—valid for up to three years—and halving post-filing expenditure review processing times from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days. At the provincial level, Québec enacted a major reform for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, replacing eight legacy innovation tax measures with the consolidated Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), which provides a 30% refundable credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D, pre-commercialization, and capital expenditures above an exclusion threshold, and 20% refundable thereafter. British Columbia fully harmonized with the federal $6,000,000 limit, ECPC expansion, and capital expenditure restoration while making its 10% credit permanent in 2026, whereas Ontario, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and the Atlantic provinces have maintained distinct expenditure caps and eligibility rules that require careful multi-jurisdictional tax modelling.

body.text: 1. Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 Historical Evolution and Policy Rationale

Federal income tax incentives for scientific research and experimental development in Canada were first introduced in 1948, with the foundational two-pronged architecture—combining an immediate or indefinitely carryforwardable income deduction with an Investment Tax Credit (ITC)—established between 1983 and 1985. As articulated by the Department of Finance Canada in the 2026 Report on Federal Tax Expenditures, the primary objective of the SR&ED program is to encourage private-sector performance of R&D in Canada and assist small and medium-sized businesses in overcoming the market failure associated with positive knowledge spillovers, where the social benefits of R&D extend beyond the performing firm to other companies and sectors of the Canadian economy. By statute, SR&ED is a non-discretionary entitlement embedded in the Income Tax Act: unlike competitive grant programs that are constrained by fixed annual budgetary envelopes, any taxpayer whose work and expenditures satisfy the statutory criteria and filing deadlines is legally entitled to claim the deduction and tax credit. According to official Department of Finance Canada and industry figures, the program supports over 23,090 to 24,160 corporate claimants and approximately 3,300 individual claimants annually (with roughly 75% being small businesses), delivering over $3 billion in federal SR&ED tax incentives each year, including $2.205 billion in projected 2024 non-refundable corporate tax credits alongside refundable transfer payments.

Prior to the 2024–2026 legislative reforms, the federal SR&ED program underwent two pivotal statutory recalibrations. First, through the Budget 2012 amendments (Jobs and Growth Act, 2012, S.C. 2012, c. 31), Parliament (i) reduced the basic ITC rate from 20% to 15% effective January 1, 2014; (ii) removed capital expenditures and equipment lease costs from the eligible expenditure base for expenditures incurred after December 31, 2013; (iii) reduced the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) for overhead from 65% of the direct salary base (applicable up to 2012) to 60% in 2013 and 55% for 2014 and subsequent taxation years; and (iv) restricted arm's-length contract SR&ED payments and third-party payments to 80% inclusion for ITC purposes effective January 1, 2013, to exclude the contractor's assumed profit element. Second, through Budget 2019, Parliament repealed the use of prior-year taxable income as a factor in phasing out a CCPC’s annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% SR&ED tax credit (effective for taxation years ending after March 18, 2019), leaving prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada as the sole phase-out metric for the CCPC expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.2). Crucially, however, prior-year taxable income was retained in the definition of "qualifying corporation" under subsection 127.1(2) for the distinct purpose of determining whether a CCPC qualifies for 40% refundability on its 15% basic ITCs earned above the expenditure limit.
1.2 Enactment of Bill C-15 (S.C. 2026, c. 3)

Following public consultations on modernizing Canada’s R&D support, the Department of Finance announced a package of SR&ED legislative proposals in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (announced in December 2024) and further expanded those enhancements in Budget 2025 (Canada Strong, tabled November 4, 2025). These measures were introduced in Parliament as Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1) and received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026 (enacted as S.C. 2026, c. 3). Under the statutory application rules, the doubled expenditure limit ($6,000,000), expanded taxable capital phase-out thresholds ($15,000,000 to $75,000,000), ECPC eligibility, and CCPC revenue-based phase-out elections apply to taxation years that begin after December 15, 2024 (i.e., on or after December 16, 2024), while the restoration of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs applies in respect of depreciable property acquired (and available for use) after December 15, 2024, and lease costs that first become payable after December 15, 2024.
1.3 Comprehensive Statutory Mapping (Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations)

The federal SR&ED regime is governed by five interlocking components of the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945). First, subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act establishes the legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development" (paragraphs (a) through (k)), alongside foundational definitions for "salary or wages", "specified employee", "property", "business", and "taxpayer". Second, section 37 of the Income Tax Act (subsections 37(1) to 37(15)) governs the computation, additions, reductions, and indefinite carryforward of the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures in computing income from a business carried on in Canada, as well as the election between the Traditional and Proxy methods, permissible foreign wage limits, specified employee salary caps, the look-through rule, and the mandatory 12-month reporting deadline for expenditures. Third, section 127 of the Income Tax Act (subsections 127(5) to 127(36)) governs the calculation and deduction of Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) against Part I tax payable, the 20-year carryforward and 3-year carryback rules, the definitions of "qualified expenditure" and "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool", the enhanced 20% credit addition, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit and phase-out formulas for CCPCs and ECPCs, non-arm's length transfers, unpaid amounts, and ITC recapture. Fourth, section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act (subsections 127.1(1) to 127.1(4)) governs the Refundable Investment Tax Credit mechanism, defining "qualifying corporation", "qualifying income limit", "excluded corporation", and the 100% and 40% refundability formulas for qualifying CCPCs, non-qualifying CCPCs, ECPCs, individuals, and trusts. Fifth, Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (sections 2900, 2901, 2902, and 2903) prescribes the rules for "directly attributable" overhead expenditures under the Traditional Method (subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3)), the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) and its overall cap and salary base limits (subsections 2900(4), 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(9)), Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) exclusions for Shared-Use Equipment (subsection 2900(11)), Prescribed Expenditures excluded from qualified expenditures (section 2902), and Special-Purpose Buildings (section 2903).

body.text: 2. Technical Eligibility Framework: Statutory Definition, the "Why" and "How" Requirements, and the Five Questions
2.1 The Statutory Definition of SR&ED (Subsection 248(1))

Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, "scientific research and experimental development" is defined as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis across four eligible categories of work (paragraphs (a) to (d)). Basic research (paragraph (a)) encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, such as studying a newly discovered virus to understand its fundamental molecular characteristics. Applied research (paragraph (b)) covers work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view, such as leveraging those identified viral characteristics to develop a vaccine mechanism. Experimental development (paragraph (c))—which represents the most commonly claimed category of SR&ED in Canada—comprises work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. The statutory phrase "including incremental improvements thereto" confirms that an eligible project does not need to create a brand-new product category; resolving a technological uncertainty to achieve a measurable, incremental advancement in an existing industrial process, software architecture, or manufacturing line fully satisfies paragraph (c).

Support work (paragraph (d)) encompasses work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to only eight exhaustive statutory categories: (1) engineering, (2) design, (3) operations research, (4) mathematical analysis, (5) computer programming, (6) data collection, (7) testing, or (8) psychological research. Support work is never SR&ED on its own; under paragraph (d), it is eligible only to the extent that it is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.
2.2 Statutory Exclusions (Paragraphs (e) to (k)) and the Purpose Distinction

The post-preamble of the definition in subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes work with respect to seven enumerated areas (paragraphs (e) to (k)), which cannot be claimed even if conducted within an innovative commercial project. These statutory exclusions are: (e) market research or sales promotion; (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities; (h) prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (j) style changes; and (k) routine data collection.

As the CRA explains in its Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives (published August 13, 2021), the decisive criterion separating eligible support work under paragraph (d) from excluded work under paragraphs (e) to (k) is purpose—that is, why the activity was performed. For example, data collection or testing performed to monitor commercial output or verify compliance with established quality assurance specifications falls under paragraphs (f) and (k) and is excluded. Conversely, non-routine data collection or destructive testing carried out specifically to test an experimental hypothesis and resolve a technological uncertainty during an ongoing SR&ED project qualifies as eligible support work under paragraph (d). Furthermore, performing excluded activities (such as mineral prospecting or commercial production runs) concurrently with SR&ED does not invalidate the eligible SR&ED work; the claimant must simply segregate and exclude the non-SR&ED work from the claim.
2.3 The CRA's "Why" and "How" Framework vs. The Common-Law Five Questions

In August 2021, the CRA replaced its former 2015 Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy with the consolidated Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. While the 2015 policy explicitly organized the analysis around a two-step structure—Step 1: Determine if there is SR&ED (using the five questions derived from Northwest Hydraulic Consultants) and Step 2: Determine the Extent of Eligible Work—the 2021 Guidelines synthesize those five questions into two overarching statutory requirements: the "Why" Requirement (Questions 1 and 4) and the "How" Requirement (Questions 2, 3, and 5).

Crucially, in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88 (affirming 2019 TCC 246), the Federal Court of Appeal rejected the taxpayer’s argument that the scientific method does not apply because those words do not appear in subsection 248(1), and in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (affirming 2020 TCC 47), the Court rejected taxpayer arguments that the CRA’s 2021 Guidelines relaxed the legal standard or removed the requirement to follow the scientific method. The FCA reaffirmed that administrative guidelines cannot alter the meaning of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, and that the five criteria established by Judge Bowman (as he then was) in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), 98 DTC 1839)—and endorsed by the FCA in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada (99 DTC 5087) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001 FCA 393)—remain the binding common-law test in Canada.
1. The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Uncertainty and Advancement — Questions 1 & 4)

Question 1 asks: Was there a scientific or technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? Scientific or technological uncertainty exists when whether a given result or objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, is not known or determined on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge or experience. As Judge Bowman held in Northwest Hydraulic and Chief Justice Rossiter reiterated in Canafric Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2023 TCC 108, para 89) and Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2024 TCC 159, para 16), the lacking knowledge must exist in the objective base of scientific or technological knowledge accessible to competent professionals in the field (combining publicly available sources and internal business resources), not merely be unknown to the claimant. Acquiring available knowledge or know-how through training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants, or purchasing proprietary knowledge or off-the-shelf tools does not constitute resolving technological uncertainty. However, system uncertainty—which arises when known technologies, components, or software architectures are combined or integrated in a complex manner such that their interactions cannot be predicted from the existing knowledge base—is a recognized form of technological uncertainty. The CRA’s 2021 Guidelines identify seven specific characteristics indicating that available technological knowledge is insufficient: (1) existing design methods are not applicable; (2) requirements or specifications do not conform to existing standards; (3) there are too many variables or unknowns; (4) parameters or conditions are outside of the normal operating range; (5) the nature of the problem is evolving; (6) data is not readily available; or (7) there are interlocking constraints, including economic or cost targets that cannot be met using known engineering approaches.

Question 4 asks: Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving (or did the process result in) a scientific or technological advancement? As clarified in Life Choice Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 21) and the CRA's Guidelines, the statutory requirement is that the work be undertaken for the purpose of generating or discovering conceptual scientific or technological knowledge (such as theories, predictive models, or new technological know-how) that advances the understanding of science or technology, rather than merely collecting factual measurements or achieving commercial novelty or increased product functionality. Importantly, failure to achieve the technical objective does not disqualify a project: if an experiment proves that a hypothesized technological approach cannot resolve the uncertainty, that negative finding still advances technological understanding. Conversely, circumventing an uncertainty through a workaround using available knowledge or terminating the investigation ends SR&ED eligibility at that point.
2. The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation, Hypotheses, and Contemporaneous Records — Questions 2, 3, & 5)

Question 2 (Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?) and Question 3 (Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis?) govern the methodology of the project. Merely following standard design protocols, systematic business processes, or unguided "trial and error" (randomly altering inputs until a result works without analysing why prior iterations failed) does not satisfy subsection 248(1). Instead, a systematic investigation or search requires four sequential elements: (1) generating an idea or hypothesis consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for investigation toward resolving the problem; (2) testing that idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis (such as building and testing experimental prototypes or simulations), allowing the hypothesis to evolve and change based on findings; (3) developing logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis, including root-cause analysis of failed tests; and (4) Question 5 (Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?), which requires maintaining contemporaneous evidence generated naturally as the work progresses—such as dated engineering notebooks, source code repositories, test logs, photographs, videos, scrap, or physical artifacts—that records the indicators measured and allows the work to be verified and repeated.

body.text: 3. Federal SR&ED Tax Incentives: Pool of Deductible Expenditures, ITC Rates, Phase-Outs, and Refundability
3.1 The Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures (Subsection 37(1))

The first of the two federal SR&ED incentives is the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures, governed by subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act and calculated in Part 3, Section C of Form T661. Unlike ordinary business expenses or standard capital cost allowance (CCA) under paragraph 20(1)(a), expenditures added to the subsection 37(1) pool form a cumulative running balance that a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may deduct in full, in part, or not at all in the current taxation year (reported on Line 460 of Form T661 and Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1), with any undeducted positive balance carried forward indefinitely (Line 470 of Form T661) to offset business income in any future taxation year. Under subsection 37(1.1), if a corporate claimant performs SR&ED related to a business actively carried on by a related corporation (such as a parent or sister corporation) at the time the expenditure is made, the SR&ED is deemed to relate to a business of the claimant.
Mechanics of Pool Additions, Reductions, Loss Restriction Events, and Partnerships

Under subsection 37(1)(a) through (c.3), the deductible SR&ED expenditure pool is increased by six statutory categories. First, paragraph 37(1)(a) adds expenditures of a current nature incurred on SR&ED carried on in Canada—comprising eligible salaries and wages (including permissible foreign wages under subsection 37(1.4)), materials consumed or transformed, equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, 100% of arm's-length and non-arm's-length SR&ED contracts performed on the claimant's behalf, 100% of eligible third-party payments, and (if using the Traditional Method) directly attributable overhead and other expenditures. Second, paragraph 37(1)(b) adds restored capital expenditures made for depreciable property (excluding land, buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings) acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, intended to be used all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time or value for SR&ED in Canada. Third, paragraph 37(1)(c) adds repayments of government or non-government assistance that previously reduced the pool under paragraph 37(1)(d). Fourth, paragraph 37(1)(c.1) adds back any amount included in the taxpayer's income in a previous taxation year under paragraph 12(1)(v) due to a negative pool balance at year-end, resetting the opening pool balance to nil (zero) for the subsequent year. Fifth, paragraphs 37(1)(c.2) and (c.3) add back federal SR&ED ITCs recaptured into tax payable in the immediately preceding taxation year under subsections 127(27), (29), (30), or (34). Sixth, pool balances transferred from a predecessor corporation on an amalgamation or from a subsidiary on a wind-up are added to the continuing corporation's pool.

Conversely, under subsection 37(1)(d) through (h), the deductible pool is reduced by: (1) government or non-government assistance (including provincial/territorial R&D tax credits and federal grants such as NRC IRAP) received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received at the filing-due date (paragraph 37(1)(d)); (2) provincial super-allowance benefit amounts (paragraph 37(1)(d.1)); (3) federal SR&ED ITCs deducted from Part I tax payable under subsection 127(5) or refunded under subsection 127.1(1) (deemed deducted under s. 127.1(3)) in the immediately preceding taxation year attributable to current expenditures or the Prescribed Proxy Amount (paragraph 37(1)(e)); and (4) amounts deducted from the pool under subsection 37(1) or section 61.3 (insolvency) in preceding years (paragraphs 37(1)(f) and (f.1)). Because prior-year federal ITCs reduce the current year's deductible SR&ED expenditure pool under paragraph 37(1)(e) (or trigger an income inclusion under paragraph 12(1)(v) if reductions exceed the pool balance), federal SR&ED ITCs are effectively brought into taxable income in the taxation year following the year they are claimed or refunded.

Under paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1), if a corporation or trust is subject to a "loss restriction event" (such as an acquisition of control of a corporation or a new majority-interest beneficiary of a trust under section 251.2), its deductible SR&ED expenditure pool is reduced to nil unless the business to which the SR&ED expenditures related is continued for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, in which case the pool may be deducted only to the extent of income from that same or a similar business. Finally, under paragraph 96(1)(e.1), a partnership cannot carry forward a pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures to a subsequent fiscal period; the partnership's entire pool balance must be deducted in calculating the partnership's net income or loss in the year incurred. For a limited partner, any portion of a partnership loss attributable to the deduction of SR&ED expenditures is denied to the limited partner, does not become a limited partnership loss or a non-capital loss, and does not affect the adjusted cost base (ACB) of the limited partner's partnership interest.
3.2 Federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Rates and Expenditure Limits (Section 127)

Under subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(10.1) of the Income Tax Act, federal SR&ED ITCs are earned at two statutory tiers. First, under paragraph (a.1) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9), all eligible claimants—including corporations, individuals (sole proprietors), partners of a partnership, and beneficiaries of trusts—earn a basic ITC rate of 15% on their "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of the taxation year (net of any provincial super-allowance benefit amount). For CCPCs and ECPCs, current-year qualified expenditures in excess of their annual expenditure limit also earn the basic 15% rate. Second, under subsection 127(10.1), if a corporation was throughout a taxation year a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) or (for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024) an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC), an additional 20% is added to the 15% basic rate—yielding an enhanced ITC rate of 35%—on the lesser of the corporation's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool for the year and its annual expenditure limit.
1. Standard CCPC Taxable Capital Formula (Subsection 127(10.2))

Under Bill C-15 (S.C. 2026, c. 3), for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit has doubled from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000. Unless a CCPC elects to use the gross revenue method under subsection 127(10.31) or 127(10.32), its expenditure limit for a particular taxation year is determined by the formula in amended subsection 127(10.2):

In this formula, A is (a) nil if the total of the CCPC's taxable capital employed in Canada for its immediately preceding taxation year—together with the taxable capital employed in Canada of each associated corporation for its last taxation year ending before the end of the CCPC's particular taxation year—is less than or equal to $15,000,000; and (b) in any other case, the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that combined prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000. Mathematically, for every $1.00 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada above $15,000,000, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit decreases by $0.10, phasing out linearly until it becomes nil ($0) at $75,000,000 of taxable capital.
2. Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and Electing CCPCs — Gross Revenue Formula (Subsections 127(9), 127(10.31), 127(10.32), and 127(10.6))

To qualify as an "eligible Canadian public corporation" at the relevant time in a taxation year under the definition added to subsection 127(9) by Bill C-15, a corporation must satisfy either paragraph (a) or paragraph (b). Under paragraph (a), the corporation must: (i) be resident in Canada; (ii) be a public corporation, or would be a public corporation if the words "designated stock exchange in Canada" in paragraph (a) of the definition of "public corporation" in subsection 89(1) were read as "designated stock exchange" (thereby encompassing Canadian-resident corporations listed on foreign designated stock exchanges, not solely Canadian exchanges); (iii) not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons; and (iv) not be a corporation that would, if each share of its capital stock owned by a non-resident person (as determined, absent actual knowledge, based on publicly available information including securities law filings made before the year) were owned by a single particular person, be controlled by that particular person. Under paragraph (b), an "eligible subsidiary" also qualifies as an ECPC if it is resident in Canada and not less than 90% of the issued shares of each class of its capital stock is owned, directly or indirectly, by one or more corporations that are ECPCs under paragraph (a).

For an ECPC—or for a standalone CCPC that files an election in the prescribed form and manner under subsection 127(10.31), or an associated group of CCPCs where all CCPCs in the group file an election under subsection 127(10.32)—the expenditure limit for a particular taxation year is determined by the formula in amended subsection 127(10.6):

Under subsection 127(10.6), A is (a) nil if the three-year average annual gross revenue over the three fiscal years immediately preceding and ending before the particular taxation year—based on the corporation's financial statements (subparagraph (a)(i)), or the consolidated financial statements of the group if the ECPC is a member of a consolidated group (subparagraph (a)(ii)), or the combined financial statement revenues of all members of an associated CCPC group (regardless of whether they were associated throughout those three years, with reasonable adjustments for intra-group sales of goods or services so that group revenue reflects a single economic entity)—is less than or equal to $15,000,000; and (b) in any other case, the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that three-year average annual gross revenue exceeds $15,000,000. This revenue election provides vital planning relief for venture-backed biotechnology, cleantech, and hardware CCPCs whose prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 due to large equity or debt financings, but whose three-year average gross revenue remains below $15,000,000.
3. Associated Corporations, Consolidated Groups, and Short Taxation Years

Under subsections 127(10.21), 127(10.3), and 127(10.61), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit must be shared among all associated CCPCs (allocated using Schedule T2SCH49) or among all ECPCs that are members of a consolidated group. However, subsections 127(10.22) and 127.1(2.2)–(2.3) provide a statutory relieving rule where two CCPCs would not be associated if paragraph 256(1.2)(a) were ignored, provided there is at least one shareholder of one corporation who is not a shareholder of the other and the Minister is satisfied that the non-overlapping share ownership was not created for the purpose of satisfying these relieving provisions. Additionally, under subsections 127(10.5) and 127(10.64)(b), where a CCPC or ECPC has a taxation year of less than 51 weeks, its expenditure limit is prorated by multiplying the otherwise-determined limit by the ratio of the number of days in the taxation year to 365 (and under paragraph 127(10.64)(c), any preceding fiscal year of less than 51 weeks used in the three-year revenue average is similarly annualized).
3.3 Refundability Rules, Carryover Periods, and ITC Recapture (Sections 127 and 127.1)

When a claimant's SR&ED ITCs exceed its federal Part I tax otherwise payable in the taxation year, the entitlement to receive the excess ITC as a cash refund is governed by section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act.
1. Refundability Rules Across Claimant Categories (Subsections 127.1(2) and 127.1(2.01))

Under subsection 127.1(2), a "qualifying corporation" is a CCPC (other than an "excluded corporation"—defined as a corporation controlled by or related to one or more tax-exempt persons under section 149, His Majesty in right of a province, a Canadian municipality, or any other public authority) whose prior-year taxable income (combined with all associated corporations) does not exceed its "qualifying income limit". Under amended subsection 127.1(2), the "qualifying income limit" is determined by the formula:

where A is nil if combined prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $15,000,000 or less, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the excess of prior-year taxable capital over $15,000,000 (phasing out to nil at $75,000,000). If a CCPC has a prior taxation year of less than 51 weeks, its taxable income for that year is annualized by multiplying by 365 ÷ days in the year under subsection 127.1(4).

A qualifying corporation is entitled under subsection 127.1(2) to: (i) 100% refundability on the unclaimed balance of its 35% enhanced ITC earned on current SR&ED expenditures and the PPA (paragraphs (f) and (g)); (ii) 40% refundability on the unclaimed balance of its 35% enhanced ITC earned on restored capital SR&ED expenditures (paragraphs (d) and (e), yielding a 14.0% cash refund and 21.0% non-refundable credit); and (iii) 40% refundability on the unclaimed balance of its 15% basic ITC earned on qualified expenditures above the expenditure limit (yielding a 6.0% cash refund and 9.0% non-refundable credit).

Conversely, for a CCPC that is not a qualifying corporation (because its prior-year taxable income exceeded its qualifying income limit) or an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) (provided neither is an excluded corporation), subsection 127.1(2.01) computes the refundable investment tax credit using the formula (40% × (A − B)) + (C − D), which grants: (i) 100% refundability (C − D) on the unclaimed balance of the 35% enhanced ITC earned on current SR&ED expenditures and the PPA; (ii) 40% refundability (40% × (A − B)) on the unclaimed balance of the 35% enhanced ITC earned on capital SR&ED expenditures; and (iii) 0% refundability (100% non-refundable) on any 15% basic ITC earned above the expenditure limit. All other corporations (foreign-controlled subsidiaries, non-ECPC public corporations, and excluded corporations) earn the 15% basic ITC on a 100% non-refundable basis. Individuals (sole proprietors) and qualifying trusts (where each beneficiary is an individual or qualifying corporation) earn the 15% basic ITC, of which 40% is refundable under subsection 127.1(2)(b)–(c). Finally, partnerships compute SR&ED ITCs at the 15% basic rate and allocate them to partners under subsection 127(8) (after deducting any partnership ITC recapture); corporate partners cannot claim the 35% enhanced rate on partnership-allocated ITCs (All Colour Chemicals).

body.text: 2. Carryback, Carryforward, and ITC Recapture (Subsections 127(5) and 127(27)–(36))

Under subsection 127(5) and the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9), any SR&ED ITC not applied against current-year Part I tax or refunded under section 127.1 (note that refunded ITCs are deemed deducted under subsection 127.1(3) and cannot be carried over) may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable, subject to acquisition-of-control restrictions.

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a claimant disposes of, or converts to commercial use, property for which an SR&ED ITC was earned—including materials for SR&ED transformed into a custom product, commercial asset, or experimental production; all or substantially all (ASA) capital equipment; Shared-Use Equipment (SUE); animals and other growing things used in SR&ED; or tangible property acquired through an SR&ED contract—the claimant must add the recaptured ITC to its Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion. The recaptured amount is the lesser of the SR&ED ITC earned in respect of the particular property and the amount calculated by multiplying the historical ITC percentage used when the credit was earned by the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value if converted to commercial use or transferred non-arm's length). If a component part is ordered from an arm's-length supplier under contract (for example, $12,000 including manufacturing and profit), the entire $12,000 contract cost is subject to recapture rules, whereas if the same component is manufactured in-house, there is no recapture on the in-house SR&ED salaries or overhead incurred to manufacture it. Disposing of or licensing intellectual property (IP) rights generated by SR&ED does not trigger ITC recapture.
4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Calculation Methods, and Specific Cost Rules
4.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method (Subsection 37(8), Subsection 37(10), and Regulation 2900)

When filing an SR&ED claim on Form T661, a claimant must choose between two statutory methods for computing SR&ED expenditures and overhead: the Proxy Method (elected by ticking Line 160 in Part 3, Section A of Form T661) or the Traditional Method (chosen by ticking Line 162, or applied automatically if the Proxy Method is not elected). Under subsection 37(10), this choice is made on a year-by-year basis when filing the first Form T661 for the taxation year and is irrevocable for that taxation year once filed.
1. The Proxy Method and the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) (Regulation 2900(4))

Under the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)), the claimant does not specifically identify, track, or allocate actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures. Instead, the claimant computes a notional amount called the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 equal to 55% of the eligible salary base under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations. Tax auditors and practitioners must note that 55% has been the statutory PPA rate since January 1, 2014 (following reductions from 65% in 2012 and 60% in 2013). Although certain unrevised lines in legacy guide summaries (such as Line 820 descriptions in older revisions of Guide T4088) still reference 65%, Regulation 2900(4) strictly mandates 55%, and applying 65% results in an immediate assessment adjustment.

The PPA is added on Line 502 in Part 4 of Form T661 to compute "qualified expenditures" that earn federal and provincial SR&ED ITCs, but the PPA is never included in the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, actual overhead expenses (office supplies, utilities, administrative/clerical support wages, non-directly engaged supervision, employer share of payroll benefits, travel, training, property taxes, and maintenance/upkeep) remain deductible as ordinary business expenses. In addition, the PPA is subject to an overall cap under the Income Tax Regulations to ensure that the sum of qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and other specified deductions does not exceed total business expenditures incurred in the taxation year.
2. The Traditional Method and the "Directly Related and Incremental" Standard (Regulation 2900(2) and 2900(3))

Under the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)), the claimant tracks, itemizes, and justifies actual "SR&ED overhead and other expenditures" on Line 360 of Form T661, which are included in both the subsection 37(1) deductible pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes. Under paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the Income Tax Regulations, an expenditure (or a reasonable portion thereof) is directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada only if it satisfies two cumulative legal tests:

items: The "Directly Related" Test: The expenditure must be directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, meaning there is a direct linkage—proceeding without deviation, interruption, or intermediary steps—between the expenditure and (i) the SR&ED work, (ii) the SR&ED staff, or (iii) the machinery or equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED.

The "Incremental" Test: The expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred. Fixed monthly charges (such as base monthly telephone, cellular, or internet fees, or fixed-cost maintenance contracts) and waste disposal costs incurred after the SR&ED activity has finished fail the incremental test.

body.text: Under subsection 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations, expenditures directly attributable to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada include: (a) the cost of maintenance and upkeep of such premises, facilities, or equipment (which is specifically allowed by Regulation 2900(3)(a) without needing to satisfy the separate directly related and incremental tests required for general overhead), and (b) other expenditures (or portions thereof) directly related to that provision that would not have been incurred had those premises, facilities, or equipment not existed.
3. Cloud Computing (AWS, Azure, GCP), GPU Infrastructure, and Software Subscriptions

A critical audit issue for software, data analytics, and artificial intelligence (AI) companies is the treatment of cloud computing costs (e.g., AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform) and software subscriptions. Under the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, materials must be physical, tangible objects (solid, liquid, or gaseous) that compose the body of a thing at a given moment in the SR&ED process; data, software licences, and cloud compute cycles are intangible and cannot be claimed as materials on Line 320 or Line 325 under either method. Furthermore, because cloud compute and software subscriptions are overhead costs, a claimant electing the Proxy Method is barred from claiming cloud invoices separately—they are replaced by the 55% PPA and will be disallowed if claimed on top of the PPA. However, under the Traditional Method, isolated cloud compute clusters or specialized software tools spun up specifically to run experimental training or testing, billed separately from standing commercial production accounts, and shut down afterward satisfy both the directly related and incremental tests under Regulation 2900(2)(c) and are 100% claimable on Line 360. Where incremental cloud compute exceeds 55% of the direct SR&ED salary base, electing the Traditional Method produces a substantially larger SR&ED claim than the Proxy Method. Additionally, where an AI or hardware firm acquires or leases physical GPU servers or compute hardware in Canada after December 15, 2024, those hardware costs are now claimable under the restored capital and lease expenditure rules.

body.text: 4.2 Salary or Wages, Specified Employee Caps, Foreign Work, and Unpaid Amounts
1. Scope of Eligible Salary or Wages and the ASA Rule

Under subsection 248(1) and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, "salary or wages" means income from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Income Tax Act (reported on a T4 slip), including base pay, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay (excluding extended vacation or sick leave), bonuses and remuneration based on profits (for non-specified employees only), inducements/non-competition payments, and taxable benefits (where there is a cash outlay or where a non-cash benefit's value is a reasonable estimate of actual cost, excluding GST/HST/PST unless no input tax credit can be claimed, and provided the actual costs are not claimed elsewhere as a business expense). Stock option benefits (excluded under subsection 143.3(2)), retiring allowances (excluded under subsection 248(1), though potentially claimable as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method if incremental), and the employer's share of related benefits (CPP, EI, worker's compensation, private health/dental plans) are excluded from SR&ED salary or wages.

Whether an employee is "directly engaged" in SR&ED is determined by the hands-on tasks performed, not the employee's job title. Eligible hands-on duties include preparing equipment and materials for experiments, conducting experimental runs and tests, recording measurements, writing experimental code, and providing direct technical supervision where the supervisor possesses a significant technological background and directs the ongoing technical course of the work (including technological planning for ongoing claimed SR&ED projects, such as assigning technological personnel, setting job priorities, developing technological strategies, and specifying the quality of materials used). Under the All or Substantially All (ASA) rule, if an employee spends 90% or more of their working time in the taxation year directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages qualifies.
2. Specified Employees: Definition, Bonus Prohibition, and Statutory YMPE Caps

A "specified employee" under subsection 248(1) is an employee who either does not deal at arm's length with the employer (under section 251) or owns, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the employer or of a corporation related to the employer. Note that in a partnership, a partner cannot be an employee of the partnership for income tax purposes; any salary or wages paid to a partner is treated as a distribution of partnership income and cannot be claimed as an SR&ED expenditure.

Specified employees are governed by three strict statutory restrictions. First, under subsection 37(9)(a), bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee are completely excluded from allowable SR&ED salary or wages. Second, under subsection 37(9.1), the maximum allowable SR&ED salary or wages expenditure that can be claimed on Line 305 of Form T661 for a specified employee (for both the Section 37 deductible pool and the qualified expenditure pool) is limited to 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual was a specified employee (5 × YMPE × B ÷ 365). Where a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, no amount may be claimed unless the associated corporations allocate the 5 × YMPE maximum among themselves by filing prescribed Form T1174 under subsections 37(9.2) and 37(9.3). Third, when computing the salary base in Part 5 of Form T661 (Boxes 850–860) to calculate the 55% PPA under the Proxy Method, subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) of the Income Tax Regulations further restrict the amount included in the salary base for a specified employee to the lesser of: (i) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (excluding bonuses, profit-based remuneration, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year; i.e., Box 854 is capped at a maximum of 75% even if the specified employee devoted 100% of their time to SR&ED); and (ii) 2.5 times the YMPE prorated by the number of days in the taxation year (2.5 × YMPE × days ÷ 365, Box 858), shared across all associated corporations employing that specified employee in the calendar year. For non-specified employees, 100% of their SR&ED time percentage is included on Line 810 of Part 5, but bonuses, profit-based remuneration, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year must still be excluded on Line 812 under Regulation 2900(9) before multiplying by 55%.
