body.text: 3. Permissible Foreign Salary or Wages (Subsections 37(1.4), 37(1.5), and 37(9)(b))

While contractor payments for SR&ED performed outside Canada are never eligible for the Section 37 pool or ITCs (they may only be deducted as current business expenses under subsection 37(2)), a claimant may claim "permissible salary or wages" on Lines 307 and 309 of Form T661 for SR&ED work carried on outside Canada if all four statutory criteria are met: (1) the foreign work is performed directly by an employee of the claimant (not a contractor); (2) the employee was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred; (3) the foreign SR&ED work was performed solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the claimant; and (4) the salary or wages paid were not subject to an income or profits tax from another country due to the employee's presence or activity abroad (subsection 37(9)(b)). Under subsection 37(1.5), the total permissible foreign salary or wages claimed on Lines 307 and 309 cannot exceed 10% of the total eligible SR&ED salary or wages for work carried on inside Canada (Line 306).
4. Unpaid Remuneration and Unpaid Non-Wage Amounts (Subsections 78(4) and 127(26))

Under subsection 78(4), if salary or wages incurred in a taxation year remain unpaid 180 days after the end of that taxation year (reported on Line 315 of Form T661), the expenditure is deemed not to have been incurred in that year; instead, it is deemed incurred in the subsequent taxation year in which the amount is actually paid (claimed on Line 310 in that subsequent year, though excluded from the Part 5 proxy salary base). Payment on the 180th day satisfies the time limit. Similarly, under subsection 127(26), non-wage SR&ED expenditures (such as contractor invoices, materials, or third-party payments) that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year are excluded from "qualified expenditures" for ITC purposes in that year (Line 520 of Form T661) and are deemed incurred for ITC purposes in the subsequent taxation year when actually paid (at the 80% rate if a contract or third-party payment).
4.3 Materials for SR&ED (Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed)

Under the CRA’s Materials for SR&ED Policy, "materials for SR&ED" means physical and tangible raw materials, substances, or other items (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that compose the body of a tangible object on which SR&ED is being carried out, that results from the SR&ED, or that is involved in testing a new or improved process. Materials may be purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers, provided they are used directly in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, and their cost may only be claimed in the taxation year in which the material is actually consumed or transformed (not when purchased or removed from inventory).

Materials consumed (Line 320) are materials destroyed or rendered virtually valueless or useless for commercial purposes as a result of the SR&ED (such as chemical reagents, substrates destroyed during testing, process water that enters a chemical reaction and is rendered valueless, or incremental animal feed, plant fertilizers, pesticides, and herbicides above normal commercial production costs). Materials transformed (Line 325) are raw materials or component parts that are changed structurally or chemically or incorporated into another physical product, prototype, custom product, or commercial asset during testing or development. If the resulting custom product, prototype, or commercial asset is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, the cost of the materials transformed is subject to ITC recapture under subsection 127(27).

The claimable cost of purchased materials is the laid-down cost (invoice price, customs and excise duties, transportation, acquisition costs, storage costs, and third-party processing services such as galvanizing required to bring a material into a condition to undergo SR&ED testing), while self-manufactured inventory includes laid-down material costs plus direct labour and production overhead under both the Traditional and Proxy methods. When materials are purchased from a non-arm's-length supplier, subsection 127(11.6) restricts the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes to the cost incurred by the non-arm's-length party (excluding any profit markup). Items that do not compose the body of the tangible object—including laboratory glassware and plastic ware (test tubes, pipettes, vials, beakers, flasks, dishes), cleaning supplies, general utilities (electricity, natural gas, oil, utility water, boiler feed water), CDs/DVDs, used lubricants, control-group animals/plants, capital property, data, and software licences—are excluded from Materials for SR&ED.
4.4 Contract Expenditures and Third-Party Payments (80% Rule, NAL Rules, and Entities A–F)
1. Arm's-Length vs. Non-Arm's-Length SR&ED Contracts (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and Subsection 127(9))

When a claimant awards a contract to a contractor to perform basic research, applied research, experimental development, or eligible paragraph (d) support work on behalf of the claimant in Canada (where the payer controls the work and typically retains ownership of the resulting IP), the tax treatment bifurcates between arm's-length and non-arm's-length performers. For arm's-length contracts (Line 340), 100% of the contract expenditure is added to the payer's subsection 37(1) deductible pool, and 80% of the contract expenditure is included in the payer's "qualified expenditures" for ITC purposes under subparagraph (a)(ii) of the definition in subsection 127(9), provided the work is performed in Canada by a "taxable supplier". To prevent double-claiming of ITCs, the amount paid or payable to the arm's-length performer is a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9) that reduces the performer's own qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(18). Where an arm's-length contract is solely for SR&ED, the CRA does not look through the contract to examine the specific categories of expenditures incurred by the performer, and following the restoration of capital expenditures after December 15, 2024, contract expenditures are no longer reduced under the subsection 37(14) look-through rule for post-December 15, 2024 depreciable capital property acquired by the performer.

For non-arm's-length (NAL) contracts (Line 345), the payer's contract expenditure is included in the payer's subsection 37(1) deductible pool, but is excluded from the payer's qualified expenditures for ITC purposes (0% ITC to payer) under paragraph (f) of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9). Instead, the amount received or receivable by the NAL performer is not considered a "contract payment", enabling the NAL performer to claim the SR&ED ITC on its own underlying expenditures (including support work), or allowing the NAL performer and payer to jointly file prescribed Form T1146 under subsection 127(13) to transfer the qualified expenditures from the performer to the payer (up to the contract amount and the performer's net qualified pool). Under the anti-avoidance rule in subsection 127(24), interposing an arm's-length intermediary between a payer and a NAL subcontractor to obtain a qualified expenditure is ineffective and disqualifies the expenditure.
2. Third-Party Payments (Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) to (iii) and Form T1263)

Unlike an SR&ED contract where services are performed on behalf of a single payer who controls the work and owns the IP as it is generated, a third-party payment (reported on Line 370 of Form T661 and detailed on Form T1263) is a payment made to a qualifying external organization to be used for SR&ED carried on in Canada related to a business of the claimant, where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results of the SR&ED. Like arm's-length contracts, 100% of a qualifying third-party payment is deductible in the subsection 37(1) pool and 80% qualifies for the federal ITC. The Income Tax Act and CRA's Third-Party Payments Policy classify recipient organizations into six statutory categories (Entities A through F):

items: Entity A (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1)): A corporation resident in Canada where the payment is used for SR&ED in Canada related to the claimant's business and the claimant is entitled to exploit the results; because paragraph 18(9)(a) (prepaid expenses) applies, the incentive is earned only in the year the SR&ED is performed.

Entities B, C, D, and E (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii)): (B) An approved association undertaking SR&ED; (C) an approved university, college, research institute, or similar institution; (D) a non-profit SR&ED corporation resident in Canada and exempt from tax under paragraph 149(1)(j); or (E) an approved organization (granting council) that makes payments to a B, C, or D entity. Because paragraph 18(9)(d) exempts these payments from the prepaid expense limitation, payments to Entities B through E earn the deduction and ITC in the taxation year the payment is paid.

Entity F (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(iii)): A payment made by a corporation to a paragraph 149(1)(j) tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporation resident in Canada for basic or applied research in Canada that has applications in other businesses unrelated to the claimant's business, where the primary purpose of the payment is for the claimant to use the results in conjunction with its own SR&ED.

body.text: 4.5 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Enacted under Bill C-15 (S.C. 2026, c. 3), capital expenditures and equipment lease costs have returned to the SR&ED regime for depreciable property acquired (and available for use under subsection 37(1.2)) after December 15, 2024, and lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024.
1. ASA Capital Expenditures (Paragraph 37(1)(b), Line 390 of Form T661)

To qualify as an allowable SR&ED capital expenditure on Line 390 of Form T661, the expenditure must result in the claimant owning (or holding a leasehold interest in) depreciable property (excluding land, inventory, goodwill, buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings under paragraph 37(8)(e)) where, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended that the property would either: (1) be used during all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada; or (2) have all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its value consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Qualifying capital expenditures claimed on Line 390 are added 100% to the subsection 37(1) deductible pool (allowing an immediate 100% deduction against income or indefinite carryforward) and must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8 (Capital Cost Allowance). Crucially, while the acquisition cost of used depreciable property meeting the ASA test after December 15, 2024 can be claimed on Line 390 and deducted in the subsection 37(1) pool, used property (property previously used, acquired for use, or leased for any purpose before acquisition by the claimant) is a prescribed expenditure under subparagraph 2902(b)(iii) of the Income Tax Regulations and must be deducted on Line 532 of Form T661, meaning used equipment does not earn an SR&ED ITC (unless refurbished prior to purchase to a "new", current state-of-the-art condition with a full new useful life, or limited strictly to the post-acquisition refurbishment costs incurred by the claimant).
2. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (Subsection 127(9), Line 504 of Form T661)

If new depreciable equipment acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 does not meet the 90% ASA test because it is shared between SR&ED and commercial activities, it may qualify as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) on Line 504 of Form T661 if it is: (1) new depreciable property; (2) not General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) (computers, hardware, software, and ancillary equipment are not GPOEF and qualify for SUE); (3) not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11) (equipment is disqualified as PDP if at acquisition the claimant intended both that it be used for SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing/processing facility, plant, or line, and that it be used over its expected useful life primarily for non-SR&ED purposes); and (4) used primarily (more than 50% and less than 90%) of its actual operating time for SR&ED in Canada during two statutory test periods.

For First-Term SUE, the test period runs from the date the property is acquired (available for use) to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that time; if actual SR&ED operating time exceeds 50% in this first period, 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (adjusted for borrowing costs under section 21, non-arm's-length costs under subsection 127(11.6), and assistance) is claimed as a qualified expenditure on Line 504 (Box 792) to earn an ITC. For Second-Term SUE, the test period runs from acquisition to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that time; if the property qualified as First-Term SUE and actual SR&ED operating time exceeds 50% in the second period, an additional 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (totalling 50% across both terms) is claimed on Line 504. The capital cost of SUE is not added to the subsection 37(1) pool; it is depreciated under regular CCA rules on Schedule T2SCH8, and any ITC claimed or refunded on SUE reduces the Undepreciated Capital Cost (UCC) of the CCA class in the subsequent taxation year.
3. Equipment Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

For equipment lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024, under the Traditional Method, if leased equipment is used ASA (90% or more of the time) for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost is claimed as a lease expenditure; if used less than 90% of the time for SR&ED, the proportional SR&ED operating percentage of the lease cost is claimable on Line 360 as an overhead expenditure, provided it is directly related and incremental. Under the Proxy Method, if leased premises, facilities, or equipment (excluding GPOEF) are used ASA (90% or more of operating time) for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost is claimable (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)); if used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90% of operating time) for SR&ED in Canada, 50% of the lease cost is claimable (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)); if used 50% or less of its operating time for SR&ED (or if the leased asset is GPOEF), 0% is claimable. Building rent is excluded under both methods unless the building is a special-purpose building as defined in Regulation 2903.
5. Government Assistance, Contract Payments, and NRC IRAP Stacking Mechanics
5.1 Statutory Rules for Assistance and Contract Payments (Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsections 127(18)–(20))

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(18) to 127(20) of the Income Tax Act, both the subsection 37(1) deductible pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool must be reduced by any "government assistance", "non-government assistance", or "contract payment" in respect of SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year. "Government assistance" under subsection 127(9) encompasses any grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax (including all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits), or investment allowance from a government, municipality, Crown corporation, or public authority, excluding the federal SR&ED ITC itself. Conditional or forgivable government loans (such as Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative [SADI] contributions where repayment is conditional on future revenues) are treated by the CRA and the courts (CAE, 2022) as assistance when received/receivable, and only increase the deductible pool under paragraph 37(1)(c) and earn non-refundable ITCs under subsections 127(10.7)–(10.8) in the future year when actually repaid. Where assistance is allocated among non-arm's-length corporations, prescribed Form T1145 must be filed under subsection 127(20).

A vital technical audit rule governs how provincial R&D tax credits interact with the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under the Proxy Method. Because provincial R&D tax credits (such as the Ontario OITC) are calculated on a base that includes both direct current expenditures and the 55% notional PPA, the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy specifies that while 100% of the provincial credit reduces federal "qualified expenditures" on Line 513 of Form T661 for ITC purposes, only the portion of the provincial credit allocated to actual current/capital SR&ED expenditures reduces the subsection 37(1) deductible pool on Line 429; the portion of the provincial credit allocated to the notional PPA does not reduce the subsection 37(1) pool, and is instead included directly in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) on Schedule T2SCH1 in the year received.
5.2 National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) and Stacking Mathematics

The National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) is Canada’s premier direct R&D grant program for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), operating for over 70 years through more than 250 Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs) across 130 offices nationwide. To qualify for NRC IRAP, an applicant must be an incorporated, profit-oriented Canadian SME with 500 or fewer full-time equivalent (FTE) employees pursuing growth and profit through the development and commercialization of innovative, technology-driven new or improved products, services, or processes in Canada. NRC IRAP provides non-repayable financial contributions reimbursing up to 80% of internal T4 employee technical salaries (for hours logged to the project) and up to 50% of eligible subcontractor costs, across funding tiers ranging from $50,000 (Accelerated Review Process) up to $10,000,000 per project, alongside Youth Employment Program (YEP) internships offering up to $30,000 per post-secondary graduate (aged 15 to 30, for 6 to 12 months).

A widespread misconception among claimants is that receiving an NRC IRAP grant cancels out SR&ED dollar-for-dollar. In reality, under the Proxy Method, the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is computed in Part 5 of Form T661 on the gross eligible SR&ED salary base before subtracting government assistance; the IRAP grant is deducted only afterward on Line 515 in Part 4 of Form T661. Consequently, every $1.00 of IRAP-reimbursed salary still generates $0.55 of notional PPA overhead on which the claimant earns both provincial and federal SR&ED tax credits.
Worked Mathematical Example: Stacking NRC IRAP + Ontario OITC/ORDTC + Federal SR&ED (Proxy Method)

Consider a qualifying Ontario CCPC (below the $15,000,000 taxable capital threshold and $500,000 taxable income threshold) that incurs $1,000,000 of eligible hands-on T4 technical salaries (non-specified employees, no bonuses) on an eligible R&D project in Ontario during its 2026 taxation year, and receives a 50% NRC IRAP grant ($500,000) on those salaries:

items: Step 1 — Gross SR&ED Expenditures & Proxy Calculation (Form T661 Parts 3 & 5): The company reports $1,000,000 in eligible SR&ED salaries on Line 300 and Line 810 (Salary Base), which generates a 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) of $550,000 on Line 502, resulting in $1,550,000 of gross qualified expenditures before assistance.

Step 2 — Subtract NRC IRAP Government Assistance (Line 515): Subtracting the $500,000 NRC IRAP grant leaves $1,050,000 ($1,550,000 − $500,000) in net qualified expenditures for Ontario provincial R&D credit purposes.

Step 3 — Compute Ontario Provincial R&D Tax Credits (OITC & ORDTC): On Schedule 566, the 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) on $1,050,000 yields $84,000 in cash. On Schedule 508, the 3.5% non-refundable Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) on the net base of $966,000 ($1,050,000 − $84,000 OITC) yields $33,810 (or the CCPC may waive the non-refundable ORDTC if it has no Ontario tax payable so as not to reduce its 35% refundable federal base).

Step 4 — Compute Federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (Line 513 & Schedule 31): Assuming both OITC ($84,000) and ORDTC ($33,810) are claimed, total provincial assistance deducted on Line 513 is $117,810, leaving a net Federal SR&ED Qualified Expenditure Pool (Line 570) of $932,190 ($1,050,000 − $117,810), on which the 35% enhanced refundable federal ITC yields $326,266.50 in cash.

Step 5 — Total Combined Funding Recovery: Combining the $500,000 IRAP grant, $84,000 OITC, $33,810 ORDTC, and $326,266.50 federal SR&ED credit yields $944,076.50 (94.41% of the $1,000,000 payroll recovered, with $910,266.50 in immediate cash). Without the $500,000 IRAP grant, the same $1,000,000 payroll ($1,550,000 gross base with PPA) would generate $124,000 OITC, $49,910 ORDTC, and $481,631.50 federal SR&ED, for a total recovery of $655,541.50 (65.55%)—proving that stacking the $500,000 IRAP grant increases net non-dilutive funding by +$288,535.00.

body.text: 6. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes (2025–2026 Audit & Alignment Analysis)

Across Canada, nine provinces (British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, Québec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Newfoundland and Labrador) and one territory (Yukon) provide R&D tax credits that stack with the federal SR&ED program, while Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not offer provincial/territorial R&D tax credits. Because every provincial or territorial R&D tax credit constitutes "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) of the federal Income Tax Act, claiming a provincial credit reduces the federal SR&ED qualified expenditure pool (and the subsection 37(1) deductible pool) unless the claimant formally renounces or waives the provincial credit by its statutory deadline. Furthermore, provincial R&D credits are earned where the permanent establishment and R&D employees actually perform the work, not where the corporation's head office is registered.
6.1 Québec: The New Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC)

In its March 25, 2025 Budget (and Information Bulletin 2025-6), the Gouvernement du Québec enacted a sweeping consolidation of its innovation tax system, replacing eight legacy tax measures with a single refundable credit: the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation — CRIC), effective for taxation years or fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025. The eliminated legacy measures (which remain available only for taxation years beginning on or before March 25, 2025) are: (1) the tax credit for salaries and wages of R&D researchers (former Form RD-1029.7, which paid 14% base or 30% enhanced); (2) the tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or research consortium (former Form RD-1029.8.6); (3) the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium (former Form RD-1029.8.9.03); (4) the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research (former Form RD-1029.8.16.1); (5) the tax credit for technological adaptation services; (6) the industrial design component of the design tax credits (the fashion design component continues); and (7) the personal income tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts.

Unlike the former Québec R&D salary credit (which phased out the 30% rate based on corporate asset size), the CRIC rate is not restricted by corporate asset size or CCPC status; every eligible corporation (or corporate member of a qualified partnership) with an establishment and carrying on business in Québec earns a fully refundable tax credit of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above the applicable exclusion threshold, and 20% (up from the former 14% base rate) on all qualified expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 limit. While Québec’s definition of R&D remains harmonized with the federal SR&ED definition (and the CRA conducts the scientific review of R&D work), the CRIC expands eligibility to pre-commercialization activities undertaken in Québec in continuation of (or conjunction with) R&D carried out in Québec by or on behalf of the corporation—specifically: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements aimed at obtaining an initial approval or certification to commercialize an innovation; and (2) product design activities, including the development of form, shape, and aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials.

Qualified expenditures under the CRIC comprise: (i) 100% of salaries and wages paid to employees for eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities in Québec; (ii) 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for contracts carried out in Québec; (iii) 50% of payments made to an eligible Québec public research centre, research consortium, or university entity; and (iv) 100% of property acquisition costs (capital expenditures) for new depreciable equipment used in Québec for R&D or pre-commercialization (excluding land, buildings, rights to use land or buildings, and property claiming the Québec C3i investment tax credit or large investment project tax holiday). Before applying the 30% and 20% rates, total qualified expenditures must be reduced by the applicable exclusion threshold, which equals the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the personal income tax basic personal amount (approximately $18,571 per employee) for each R&D and pre-commercialization employee, prorated for the percentage of time spent by each employee on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities. The CRIC is claimed by filing Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (RD-1029.8.CR, Codes 112 and 113) with Revenu Québec. Separately, Québec IT firms should note that the CDAE (30% of eligible IT salaries: 23% refundable + 7% non-refundable in 2025) is replaced for fiscal years starting after December 31, 2025 by the CDAEIA (for corporations significantly integrating AI features, at 30% above an exclusion threshold: 22% refundable + 8% non-refundable in 2026), and Québec’s DICI IP box taxes eligible IP commercialization income at 2% instead of 11.5%.
6.2 Ontario: Three-Tiered System (OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC)

Ontario administers three corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) via the CRA and the T2 return. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96, Schedule T2SCH566) provides an 8% fully refundable credit (reduced from 10% on June 1, 2016) on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures per associated group (maximum annual refund of $240,000). As of late 2026, Ontario has not aligned the OITC with the federal $6,000,000 expenditure limit; the OITC cap remains $3,000,000, and it phases out when prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or when prior-year specified capital (taxable paid-up capital) is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. As set out in the 2026 Ontario Economic Outlook and Fiscal Review (October 29, 2026), Ontario has, however, restored the eligibility of certain capital expenditures on property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 for both the OITC and the ORDTC, a change that took effect automatically in Ontario when Bill C-15 received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Sections 38 to 45, Schedule T2SCH508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable credit (reduced from 4.5% on June 1, 2016) on all eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (reduced by any OITC claimed), with no expenditure cap, a 3-year carryback, a 20-year carryforward, and the right to deliver a written waiver within 6 months of tax year-end. Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97, Schedules T2SCH568 & T2SCH569) provides a 20% fully refundable credit on qualified expenditures incurred in Ontario under an eligible contract with an eligible Ontario research institute, capped at $20,000,000 of expenditures ($4,000,000 maximum credit) per associated group.
6.3 British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Atlantic Provinces, and Yukon

items: British Columbia (Sections 97 to 103 of the Income Tax Act (British Columbia), Form T666): British Columbia expressly aligned with the federal Bill C-15 reforms for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, increasing the expenditure limit for its 10% refundable SR&ED credit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 ($600,000 maximum annual refund), aligning its taxable capital phase-out range to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extending the 10% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) alongside CCPCs, restoring post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures, and making the BC credit permanent in BC Budget 2026. Expenditures above $6,000,000 or by other corporations earn a 10% non-refundable credit (3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward), and Form T666 must be filed within 18 months of tax year-end.

Alberta (Sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act, Forms AT1 Schedule 29 & AT4970): Operates independently through the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), which provides an 8% fully refundable benefit on eligible Alberta R&D expenditures up to the corporation's two-year average historical base spending, plus an additional 12% refundable benefit (20% combined refundable rate) on incremental spending above that two-year base. Per June 30, 2026 technical guidance, Alberta did not adopt the federal $6,000,000 limit or federal capital expenditure restoration, retaining its $4,000,000 annual expenditure cap, its $10,000,000–$50,000,000 taxable capital phase-out, and its filing deadline of 15 months after the AT1 filing-due date.

Saskatchewan (Sections 63 to 63.4 of The Income Tax Act (Saskatchewan), Schedule T2SCH403): For qualifying expenditures incurred on or after December 16, 2024, Saskatchewan doubled its CCPC refundable expenditure limit from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 (yielding up to $200,000 at the 10% refundable rate for CCPCs), while expenditures above $2,000,000 or incurred by non-CCPCs earn a 10% non-refundable credit (3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward), subject to a $1,000,000 total annual combined credit cap.

Manitoba (Section 7.3 of The Income Tax Act (Manitoba), Schedule T2SCH380): Provides a 15% credit on eligible Manitoba R&D expenditures (including current expenditures and non-building depreciable capital property), of which 50% (7.5% effective rate) is refundable and 50% (7.5% effective rate) is non-refundable (3-year carryback, 20-year carryforward) for in-house R&D, or 100% refundable (15%) when contracted with an eligible Manitoba research or educational institution (with educational institution contracts included at 100% rather than 80%).

Nova Scotia (s. 41 Income Tax Act (Nova Scotia), Schedule T2SCH340), New Brunswick (s. 59 New Brunswick Income Tax Act, Schedule T2SCH360), Newfoundland and Labrador (s. 42 Income Tax Act (Newfoundland and Labrador), Schedule T2SCH301 / Form T1129), and Yukon (s. 15 Income Tax Act (Yukon), Schedule T2SCH442 / Form T1232): All four jurisdictions provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit to all eligible corporations (and to individuals in NL and Yukon) with no expenditure cap, plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) in Yukon on amounts paid or payable to Yukon University, while Newfoundland and Labrador uniquely does not reduce its provincial expenditure base by government or non-government assistance (except GST/HST input tax credits). Because provincial credits reduce the federal SR&ED expenditure base, in a 15% refundable province such as Nova Scotia, $1,000,000 of qualified current expenditures yields a $150,000 provincial cash refund and reduces the federal base to $850,000, generating $297,500 at the 35% federal rate for a 44.75% ($447,500) combined cash recovery for a CCPC/ECPC, or 27.75% ($277,500) for a foreign-controlled subsidiary ($150,000 cash + $127,500 non-refundable federal credit).

body.text: 7. Governing Bodies, Prescribed Forms, Filing Deadlines, Pre-Claim Approval (PCA), and CRA Audit Procedures
7.1 Governing Authorities and Prescribed Forms (May 2026 Revisions)

In Canada, the Department of Finance Canada formulates R&D tax policy and legislation, while the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers the federal SR&ED program (and all provincial/territorial R&D tax credits except Québec's CRIC, which is administered financially by Revenu Québec, and Alberta's IEG, which is administered by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance). Within the CRA, technical eligibility reviews are conducted by Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) (reporting to a Research and Technology Manager [RTM]), while expenditure and accounting verifications are conducted by Financial Reviewers (FRs) (reporting to a Financial Review Manager [FRM]).

To claim federal SR&ED incentives, a taxpayer must file Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, guided by publication Guide T4088) together with Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) for corporations or Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit – Individuals) for individuals and trusts. Following the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, the CRA released updated prescribed forms in May 2026 (Form T661, Form T1145, and Form T1146 updated May 15, 2026; Schedule T2SCH31 updated May 22, 2026; and Schedule T2SCH49 updated May 29, 2026).

On the updated Form T661 (Version T661(26)), Part 1 captures general claimant and partnership information (Lines 010–157). Part 2 captures project-by-project technical descriptions across Section A (Project title on Line 200, start/completion dates on Lines 202–204, new Line 207 requiring the five-digit Field of Research code (entered with the prefix RDF) from Statistics Canada's Canadian Research and Development Classification 2020 Version 2.0, and new Lines 212 & 214 for the Pre-Claim Approval indicator and Case Number), Section B (Line 242 for scientific or technological obstacles/uncertainties, Line 244 for work performed in the tax year to overcome them, and Line 246 for scientific or technological advancements achieved; for national security "classified information" projects, Section B is kept on a separate sheet on file and a notification letter is mailed to the CRA Business Tax Incentives Directorate in Ottawa), and Section C (Personnel on Lines 253–261, new Line 262 listing the names of the 10 most expensive SR&ED depreciable properties acquired after December 15, 2024 and claimed on Line 390, new Line 263 entering the percentage of total operating time for each property on Line 262, foreign/contract indicators on Lines 265–269, and the contemporaneous evidence checklist on Lines 270–282). Part 3 covers the Traditional/Proxy election (Lines 160/162), allowable current and capital expenditures (Lines 300–400, including Line 390 for restored ASA capital expenditures), and the subsection 37(1) deductible pool (Lines 429–470). Part 4 computes qualified expenditures for ITC purposes (Lines 500–570, including Line 502 for the PPA, Line 504 for SUE acquired after December 15, 2024, and new/updated Lines 518, 532, 535, and 540 for capital assistance, prescribed expenditures including used property, other capital deductions, and allocated excess assistance). Part 5 computes the salary base and 55% PPA (Lines 810–820, Boxes 850–860); Part 6 allocates project costs across Boxes 750–792 (including Box 782 for ASA capital cost and Box 792 for 25% SUE cost); Part 7 reports expenditures for statistical purposes (Line 605); Part 8 is the claim checklist; Part 9 captures mandatory Claim Preparer Information; and Part 10 is the officer certification.
7.2 Statutory Reporting Deadlines and Absolute Preclusion (Subsections 37(11)–(12) and Paragraph 127(9)(m))

Under subsection 37(11) (for expenditures) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) (for ITCs), a claimant must file the prescribed forms (Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND)) containing the prescribed information on or before the day that is 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. Because a corporation's T2 return due date is 6 months after its taxation year-end, the corporate SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of the taxation year (for individuals, 17.5 months after year-end; for partnerships, Form T661 must be filed no later than 12 months after the earliest filing-due date for the return of income of any member of the partnership for the fiscal period). Under subsection 37(12), if a taxpayer fails to file the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information by this 12-month reporting deadline, the expenditures cannot be characterized or claimed as SR&ED expenditures or earn ITCs for that year. The Income Tax Act provides no statutory mechanism or ministerial discretion to extend this deadline, and taxpayer relief under subsection 220(3.1) cannot revive a late-filed Form T661 or a missing Schedule T2SCH31 (Datacalc Research, 2000; Easyway Cattle, 2015 TCC 211; Westsource, 2017 TCC 9). Supporting books and records must be retained for six years from the end of the last taxation year to which they relate under paragraph 230(4)(b).
7.3 The Elective Pre-Claim Approval (PCA) Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

Introduced in Budget 2025 and officially launched by the CRA on April 1, 2026, the optional Pre-Claim Approval (PCA) process allows eligible businesses—specifically CCPCs, Canadian corporations, and Canadian partnerships that have annual gross income of less than $25,000,000 and are in good standing with the CRA—to obtain upfront technical approval of their planned R&D projects before starting work or incurring costs. The PCA process operates in four sequential steps:

items: Step 1 — Open a PCA Request: Complete the online web form (taking under 5 minutes) to receive a Pre-Claim Approval Case Number within 2 to 5 business days.
Step 2 — Apply in My Business Account: Complete the formal application in My Business Account within a few hours using existing project documentation for up to three (3) projects.

Step 3 — Meet with a CRA SR&ED Specialist: Within four (4) weeks of submitting the application, the CRA contacts new SR&ED claimants to schedule a mandatory meeting with an SR&ED specialist (and may schedule a meeting with existing claimants in good standing).

Step 4 — Receive Official Determination: Within eight (8) weeks of completing the application in My Business Account, the CRA issues an official Pre-Claim Approval determination, which is valid for up to three (3) years. When the annual SR&ED claim is subsequently filed (entering the Case Number on Lines 212 and 214 of Form T661), if the claim is selected for an expenditure review, the CRA’s processing timeline is cut in half from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days (unless the actual project differed significantly from what was approved or unapproved projects were added to the claim).

body.text: 7.4 CRA Claim Review Process, Penalties (Subsections 162(5.1) and 163(2)), and Dispute Resolution

For refundable SR&ED claims accepted without review, the CRA’s processing standard is 60 calendar days (and up to 120 days for payment); for refundable claims selected for technical and financial review, the service standard is 180 calendar days from receipt of a complete claim (90% target; 90 days for PCA expenditure-only reviews; no service standard for non-refundable claims under review). As detailed in The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated July 2, 2025), a CRA review follows three stages: Step 1 (Start of Review), where the RTA or FR phones the claimant, sends an initial letter with a meeting agenda, and issues any pre-meeting information request (with a standard 30-day deadline); Step 2 (Review Meeting & Information Requests), conducted virtually (or on-site by exception) to interview technical and financial staff, tour the facilities, examine contemporaneous technical and financial records, and share preliminary findings; and Step 3 (End of Review & Proposal Package), where—if adjustments are proposed—the CRA sends a Proposal Package containing the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, a Proposal Letter summarizing proposed expenditure/ITC adjustments and any penalties, and detailed tax calculations, giving the claimant 30 days to submit written representations before a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued.

Two statutory penalty regimes require strict compliance attention. First, under subsections 162(5.1) to 162(5.3), if complete and accurate Part 9 Claim Preparer Information is not provided on Form T661, a $1,000 penalty applies for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally liable (though the SR&ED claim itself is not disallowed solely due to missing Part 9 data, and Part 9 is not subject to the 18-month reporting deadline). Second, under subsection 163(2) (paragraphs 163(2)(a) and (d)) and the CRA’s Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025), where the CRA establishes on a balance of probabilities (carrying the burden of proof under subsection 163(3)) that a person knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence made or participated in a false statement or omission in an initial or amended SR&ED claim, the penalty equals the greater of $100 or 50% of the sum of: (1) the understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission (with overstated pool expenditures and overstated ITCs deemed deducted first, and taxable income deemed not less than zero under subsection 163(2.1)), plus (2) the refund of the overstated refundable ITC claimed. Crucially, once the gross negligence penalty applies to a refundable ITC claim, the CRA calculates the 50% penalty on the entire overstated refundable ITC, even if part of the overstatement stemmed from a simple oversight or misunderstanding of the Act. If disputes cannot be resolved through the CRA’s three-step administrative dispute resolution process (1. Reviewer, 2. Manager [RTM/FRM], 3. Administrative Review), the claimant may file a formal Notice of Objection after assessment/reassessment and subsequently appeal to the Tax Court of Canada (under the Informal or General Procedure) and the Federal Court of Appeal.
8. Comprehensive Jurisprudence and Case Law Audit (1997–2026)

In Canadian tax litigation, an appeal to the Tax Court of Canada is an appeal on the merits (de novo) regarding whether the work satisfies subsection 248(1), rather than a judicial review of how the CRA conducted its audit (Life Choice Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 21). Furthermore, the taxpayer bears the burden of demolishing the factual assumptions pleaded by the Minister of National Revenue in the Reply by presenting a prima facie case supported by objective evidence (Canada v. Loewen, 2004 FCA 146; Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada, 2026 FCA 175).
8.1 Foundational and Modern Appellate Jurisprudence (1998–2026)

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839, Judge Bowman (as he then was) allowed the taxpayer’s appeal regarding physical scale hydraulic modelling and formulated the foundational Five Criteria for SR&ED eligibility, establishing that system uncertainty can arise when known components are combined in a novel way, that incremental advancements and unsuccessful experiments qualify, and that adherence to the scientific method separates SR&ED from routine engineering. The Federal Court of Appeal adopted Judge Bowman’s criteria as binding law in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada, [1998] F.C.J. No. 1890 (QL), [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA) (holding that while testing and repeatability are essential, the death of a key witness or absence of a rigid paper format can be overcome by reliable oral and circumstantial evidence of systematic testing) and summarized the five-question framework in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393. Earlier, in Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen, 97 DTC 724 (TCC), the Tax Court affirmed that SR&ED provisions should be interpreted purposively to encourage research in Canada and allowed materials transformed during experimental textile production runs.

Between 2021 and October 2026, three landmark Federal Court of Appeal decisions reinforced the evidentiary and methodological rigour required in SR&ED appeals. First, in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, the FCA rejected the taxpayer’s argument that because the words "scientific method" do not appear in the text of subsection 248(1), the criterion should not apply; the Court held that following the scientific method is an essential judicial interpretation of a "systematic investigation or search... by means of experiment or analysis". Second, in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (affirming 2020 TCC 47), the FCA dismissed a software developer's appeal, holding that (1) the CRA’s August 13, 2021 Guidelines did not remove the requirement to follow the scientific method, which the Tax Court applied flexibly in a manner suitable for applied sciences and software, and (2) the Tax Court properly excluded the taxpayer’s expert witness report because it failed to comply with the Code of Conduct for Experts and improperly opined on the ultimate legal question of whether the work constituted SR&ED. Third, in Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada, 2026 FCA 175 (decided October 21, 2026; affirming 2025 TCC 183), the taxpayer appealed the disallowance of 13 of 14 food-processing projects from the 2005–2009 taxation years, arguing that because the Tax Court judge found its sole witness credible and the Crown called no competing witness, the Minister's assumptions were displaced. The FCA dismissed the appeal with costs, holding that finding a witness credible does not automatically establish that the work satisfies the legal criteria for SR&ED. Believing a witness is honest is legally distinct from finding that their testimony provides sufficient substantive evidence to prove an objective gap in industry knowledge, formulated hypotheses, and systematic experimentation rather than trial and error; moreover, the Crown is not required to call a competing witness and may rely on deficiencies in the taxpayer's own documents and cross-examination.
8.2 Recent Tax Court of Canada Precedents Across Key Sectors (2015–2026)

In the food science and processing sector, two major Tax Court decisions illustrate how claimants can defeat CRA allegations of "routine trial and error". In Canafric Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2023 TCC 108, Chief Justice Rossiter allowed the appeal of a frozen meat pie manufacturer for projects between 2013 and 2016 aimed at extending shelf life and preserving structural integrity after freezing/reheating without chemical preservatives and with reduced salt and fat. The Court rejected the CRA’s characterization of the work as trial and error because, after each failed batch, the claimant "conducted analyses in order to understand which requirement was not met" and adjusted subsequent formulations scientifically, supported by a combination of documentary and testimonial evidence. Building directly on Canafric, in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2024 TCC 159 (Amended Reasons issued January 17, 2025, Docket 2023-2126(IT)I), Justice Bodie allowed the taxpayer's appeal for the 2020 taxation year regarding the development of "Chrisoda", an unpasteurized cold-pressed juice product targeting a two-year room-temperature shelf life (where early test batches suffered microbial fermentation that caused cans to explode), holding that achieving non-refrigerated two-year stability without pasteurization posed a genuine technological uncertainty beyond standard industry practice.

In the software, engineering, and manufacturing sectors, recent Tax Court jurisprudence draws a sharp boundary between system-level architectural uncertainty and standard engineering. In Dazzm Inc. v. The Queen, 2024 TCC 129, the Tax Court allowed the taxpayer's software claim involving cloud-based SaaS integration and React performance bottlenecks, complementing earlier software taxpayer wins in ACSIS EHR Inc. v. The Queen, 2016 TCC 50 (software stability), E-Nor, 2018 (data analytics methodologies), and CRL Engineering, 2019 TCC 65 (distributed computing). In Willowglen Systems Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2026 TCC 7, the Tax Court issued a split decision, disallowing a SCADA software upgrade as routine software engineering while allowing the experimental development of a high-assurance Safety Integrity Level 4 (SIL 4) train-control box. Similarly, in manufacturing and industrial engineering, taxpayers prevailed where structured experimentation and technological advancement were proven—including 6379249 Canada Inc., 2015 TCC 77 (printer design problems post-commercial sale and proof a project was filed), General Motors of Canada, 2017 (automotive manufacturing process improvements and material testing), Formadrain, 2017 TCC 42, A&D Precision, 2019 TCC 48, Béton Mobile, 2019 CCI 278, and Buhler, 2023 TCC 18 (tractor design)—whereas claims lacking technological uncertainty beyond standard practice were dismissed in Jentel Manufacturing (2015), Tawa Developments (2015), PharmEng Technology (2013), Indusol Industrial Control (2020 TCC 103), WRD Borger Construction (2021 TCC 40), and Vortex Energy Services Ltd. (2025 TCC 63), with a split outcome in Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. (2025 TCC 173) (addressing industrial heating elements, statute-barred years, and s. 163(2) penalties). On financial and structural issues, key rulings include AG Shield (2017 TCC 68) and Oldcastle (2016 CCI 183) (upholding reasonable SR&ED wage allocations), André Lamy MPC (2020 TCC 61) (directly engaged test), and Mindready Solutions (2015 CCI 17), Aeronautic Development Corp. (2017 TCC 39), and CO2 Solution Technologies (2019 CCI 286) (loss of CCPC status and the 35% enhanced rate due to de facto or public company control).

body.text: 9. Strategic Compliance Checklist for Canadian R&D Claimants (2026–2027)

To maximize non-dilutive recovery and insulate claims from CRA audit adjustments under the enacted Bill C-15 regime, Canadian corporations and tax advisors should execute the following eight-step compliance protocol:

items: Apply for Pre-Claim Approval (PCA) Before Commencing Major Projects: For CCPCs, Canadian corporations, and Canadian partnerships with under $25,000,000 in annual gross income, submit the online PCA web form and My Business Account application for up to three core R&D projects prior to incurring expenditures to obtain a binding 8-week technical determination (valid for up to 3 years) and cut post-filing expenditure review times from 180 days to 90 days.

Model the Subsection 127(10.31)/(10.32) Gross Revenue Election vs. Taxable Capital: For capital-intensive CCPCs whose prior-year associated taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000 (due to equity or debt financings) but whose three-year average annual gross revenue is below $15,000,000 (or lower than their taxable capital), file the prescribed election under subsection 127(10.31) or 127(10.32) to preserve the full $6,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit.

Verify ECPC Qualification for Publicly Listed Canadian Innovators: Canadian-resident public companies listed on Canadian or foreign designated stock exchanges (and their ≥90%-owned Canadian subsidiaries) should audit their shareholder registers and public securities filings under subsection 127(9) to confirm non-control by non-residents and claim the newly enacted 35% refundable ITC on up to $6,000,000 of expenditures.

Perform Annual Arithmetic Modelling of Traditional vs. Proxy Method for AI/Cloud Teams: Never default automatically to the 55% Proxy Method (Line 160). If incremental, separately billed cloud compute costs (AWS/Azure/GCP experimental GPU training clusters) plus employer payroll benefits and sub-90% equipment leases exceed 55% of the direct SR&ED salary base—or if adding actual overhead to the Section 37 deductible pool is advantageous—elect the Traditional Method on Line 162 before filing Form T661.

Capitalize on Restored Capital and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) Rules (Post-December 15, 2024): Track operating-time logs for all new depreciable laboratory, manufacturing, and GPU/compute hardware acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024. Claim equipment used ≥90% in SR&ED on Line 390 (and list the 10 most expensive properties and their operating time percentages on new Lines 262 and 263), and claim new equipment used >50% to <90% in SR&ED as First-Term and Second-Term SUE (25% + 25%) on Line 504.

Optimize Québec CRIC Pre-Commercialization and Equipment Claims (Post-March 25, 2025): For operations in Québec, expand project tracking beyond pure SR&ED to capture regulatory validation/certification testing and product design (form, aesthetics, functionality, material choice) flowing from Québec R&D, and bundle eligible expenses to maximize utilization of the 30% refundable CRIC tier on the first $1,000,000 above the exclusion threshold on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T.

Structure Contemporaneous Technical Records Around Root-Cause Failure Analysis: In accordance with Canafric (2023 TCC 108), Manning Canning (2024 TCC 159), and Tuna Temple (2026 FCA 175), ensure engineering logs, Git/Jira repositories, and test records explicitly document the baseline industry knowledge gap, the causal hypothesis formulated prior to each test, the quantitative indicators measured, and the root-cause analysis of why failed iterations did not meet target specifications.

Enforce Strict Calendar Controls for the 180-Day Unpaid Rule and the 18-Month Reporting Bar: Pay all accrued SR&ED wages, bonuses (for non-specified employees), and contractor invoices within 180 days of fiscal year-end (subsections 78(4) and 127(26)), verify Part 9 claim preparer disclosures to avoid the $1,000 subsection 162(5.1) penalty, and file complete Form T661, Schedule T2SCH31, and provincial schedules well ahead of the non-extendable 18-month statutory deadline under subsection 37(11).
